title: Introducing Gemini Omni
transcriptText:
NICOLE BRICHTOVA: There are so
many different kinds of edits
that you can do, and I
think we weren't sure
what exactly the model
was going to pick up on.
But it actually
is very versatile.
We have an amazing
group of people
who have been making demos
for the past couple of weeks,
and I've been really blown away
with all the kinds of things
that they have been
able to do, of, like,
turning themselves into crochet
dolls, and liquefying things.
And those things--
and they just work,
and it's all through prompting,
which is pretty incredible.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
LOGAN KILPATRICK: Hey, everyone.
Welcome back to "Release Notes."
My name is Logan Kilpatrick.
I'm on the Google DeepMind team.
Today, I'm joined by
Nicole, Dumi, Gabe, Shlomi.
We're talking about
the new Omni model--
Gemini Omni.
So maybe one of you want
to sort of kick us off
with the high level
news about the model.
NICOLE BRICHTOVA: We're
really excited to introduce
Gemini Omni.
I think there's two things
that people should take away
from this model.
One is we're basically
bringing Nano Banana to video.
So we have a really great
video generation model,
but it especially
shines at video editing.
And the second thing, the
reason we're calling it Omni,
is it's really the next step
towards the journey of making
Gemini fully multimodal
in and multimodal out.
So you can take in image,
video, audio input, references,
and, right now, good
video as output.
And then in the future, we
will be adding more modalities
as a way to make Gemini
fully multimodal in and out.
LOGAN KILPATRICK: I love it.
I feel like we've been telling
the Gemini multimodal input
story.
It was sort of a foundational
part of the original Gemini
models.
And then, obviously, the whole
suite from Nano Banana to Veo
to some of the music
and audio models,
like state-of-the-art across the
rest of the gen media portfolio.
So it's exciting to see
it all come together.
Maybe we look at
demos and see, and we
can do some live reactions.
NICOLE BRICHTOVA: Let's
go to some examples.
Let's play this one.
So this is actually
a really nice example
of bringing together the
Gemini world knowledge
media generation.
And so this is literally
asking the model
to generate the
alphabet and then
examples of an object for
each letter of the alphabet.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
LOGAN KILPATRICK: Nice.
And how aware is the model of
its own-- because I imagine
there's a time constraint
of how much generation
the model can do.
Is it aware of its own time?
Is the speed
sequence, do we have
to prompt the model to be
make sure to do it fast
because you only have
8 seconds to generate?
Or how much of that context is--
SHLOMI FRUCHTER: I think that's
one of the things that really
improved on, is that
the model has an ability
to create very fast,
potentially sequences.
So unlike previous
generations of our models,
the control over the time and
being able to tell a story
is much better.
This is a bit of an
extreme kind of situation
where you want to create
very fast frames that
go one after the other.
Each one has different content,
and there is a specific order,
so the model is very
aware temporally
where everything should go.
And basically, when the user
asks for a relatively kind
of complex sequence, then the
model is able to reason about it
and create the
sequence correctly.
DUMITRU ERHAN: To your question
about do you have to prompt it,
you can, but you don't have to.
It's pretty flexible
in that sense.
You can just say, well,
I do it in ten seconds,
and it will do it.
But you can also
specify, well, I
want it to be slow mo, whatever
it is that you want it to.
So it's pretty
controllable in that sense.
GABE BARTH-MARON: Part of that
comes from the conditioning.
So there's this
text conditioning
that goes into the model.
Should it be fast paced?
Should it be really slow?
But then another part of it
is just from the model itself.
It really looks to
find these correlations
between what you're asking for
and how the video should look.
LOGAN KILPATRICK:
Yeah, I love it.
There's an AI video speed.
That first example
is like cool to see
that it is a lot faster paced
than what you would normally
get out an AI video
generator, which is cool.
NICOLE BRICHTOVA: And this
one's very fast paced,
and we prompted it
to be very fast paced
to fit the alphabet in.
But we have another example,
which goes into the editing
capabilities and
also the anything in,
because we're using an image
as input and a video as input.
So let's play a video
of this woman talking.
[VIDEO PLAYBACK]
- Well, I don't know
what it is, but today
is going to be a good day.
I can feel it.
[END PLAYBACK]
NICOLE BRICHTOVA: This is Irina,
one of our amazing creators
on the Greenfield team.
And then the prompt is basically
turn me into this animal.
[VIDEO PLAYBACK]
- Well, I don't know
what it is, but today
is going to be a good day.
I can feel it.
[END PLAYBACK]
LOGAN KILPATRICK:
That's awesome.
Just to draw it
back to folks who
have some familiarity
with the Veo models,
this is a combination of
reference to video audio.
And the part that
wasn't possible
before is the audio consistency.
Because you could do editing
like that with previous Veo
generations, right with
reference to Veo or no?
Or is that not possible?
NICOLE BRICHTOVA: You
could do a reference
to video, where the reference
was an image or an audio clip.
But video editing
is a net new thing
that we're bringing with Omni.
And that's why we like
to use the reference
it's kind of Nano
Banana for video,
because we're basically
combining everything
that we had in
Veo and also Omni,
and we're adding video editing.
And it's really nice because
with Gemini in the loop
again, because we're
building on Gemini,
you can use fairly
simple language.
Literally, turn me
into this animal.
There's nothing that
complex in the prompt,
and then the model just does it.
And then it keeps
the voice the same
and it keeps the speech the
same, which is really nice.
SHLOMI FRUCHTER:
Yeah, we pretty much
build them all
from the ground up
to be able to understand
different modalities,
so in this case, the
image and the video.
So it can actually
know what information
it has to take from the source
or, in this case, the reference
video which a person is
talking and recontextualize it.
In this case, it's
an animal talking.
But I think the small
movements, the expressions
of the animal kind of transfer
from the original person.
And I think, really, those
nuances make it look better.
GABE BARTH-MARON: Yeah, I think
that's a really important point,
is that while you could
certainly do reference to video,
that was the capability that
we almost layered into it.
Whereas with Omni, it's
really a step change.
It's like we started
from the foundation.
We had to rethink how to build
this model from the ground up.
And we're really happy with
the results because of that.
DUMITRU ERHAN: Maybe
pragmatically also,
like it actually does improve
the quality-- improves
with more references that you
put in of the same subject.
So you can stuff in
more images of yourself
and more whatever
it is, and it will
build a better model--
world model if you
want to use the term of art.
And it will just be
a better outcome.
SHLOMI FRUCHTER: We can also
talk a bit more about the way
to provide them all
with your references.
So we have the Avatar
workflow, which
we'll be talking about more,
that allows you to just one time
take a photo of yourself, and
speak, and get the sample,
and then use it across
different generations.
But also, it can bring 3 or 4
or even more-- up to, I think,
about 7--
other references of yours
and voice references.
And again, the more
information that the model has,
the more it can recreate
and recontextualize
the presence of this
specific person or identity
in a new scene.
And I think what we've
seen is that it's also
not just the number
of references,
but also what information
the references have.
So, for example, if I take a few
photos of myself from different
angles, the model can build a
better understanding of the 3D
structure of the face.
And then, if you
walk around, then it
will actually look
more like you, right?
If you only have a
front photo of yourself,
then when you turn around, it
might look a different person,
because the model has no idea
how you look from the side.
So it's also about that.
GABE BARTH-MARON: And it's
important to point out
that these references don't have
to be the same thing or person.
So you can have two people.
Or in this case, we
saw there was a wolf,
but you could have even multiple
animals, whatever you wanted.
And then in your prompt, you
just point back to the things
that you want to
incorporate into the video,
and it will just
intuitively just figure out
what to do with those.
LOGAN KILPATRICK:
Yeah, that's awesome.
Let's look at some more demos.
I feel like we've got lots
of cool ones to look through.
NICOLE BRICHTOVA:
We have an image
of a violin on this background
which is just grass,
and then we have a
woman playing a violin.
And the first prompt is
basically take this violinist
and transport her
into this environment.
So let's play that.
[VIDEO PLAYBACK]
[VIOLIN PLAYING]
[END PLAYBACK]
Our next prompt is make
the violin invisible
and then keep everything
else the same, right?
So let's see what happens.
[VIDEO PLAYBACK]
[VIOLIN PLAYING]
[END PLAYBACK]
LOGAN KILPATRICK:
That's awesome.
Wow.
NICOLE BRICHTOVA:
It's really awesome
because it keeps
everything else the same.
She looks the same.
She's still playing,
the music is the same,
and then the violin
just disappears
and you see what happens.
And then this next one
is basically change
the perspective.
So you can see
how this is useful
for many different
things, and it would
have been really hard to do.
And you can also see
how the model just
is an understanding
of perspective
and what happens when
you change camera angles.
So let's play this one.
[VIOLIN PLAYING]
I do not play the violin, but
I am told this looks right.
LOGAN KILPATRICK: Yeah for sure.
That's awesome.
Actually, really
quickly, on multi-turn, I
think one of the pieces of early
feedback from the original Nano
Banana models was sort like
when you do multi-turn,
sometimes the model actually
wouldn't make the edits.
We see that feedback all
the time from people,
and it's gotten
progressively better.
And I'm curious just to level
set people's expectation as they
go in and try this model.
Is it pretty consistent it'll
make the changes that you want,
or does it still have
that odd artifact
that Nano Banana has sometimes,
where you'll ask for it
and it'll end up just giving
you the same image back
without anything really changed?
NICOLE BRICHTOVA:
It's less that.
I think the main difference
is between Nano Banana
and Omni here is obviously the
generations take a lot longer.
So Nano Banana was super snappy.
You have ten seconds and
then you get the output.
Here, you're probably
waiting like 60 seconds plus,
sometimes 90.
So I think that
naturally maybe limits
how much you want
to do multi-turn.
But it definitely-- I think the
other thing is that we've seen
this with Nano Banana, too.
Obviously, the
longer you go, maybe
the more the instruction
following degrades,
and that's still true.
But we've been getting
2, 3, 4 turns pretty
reliably with this model.
But I think to
your point, I think
every time we introduce
new capabilities like this,
sometimes the model is better
at following some instructions
than others.
So please send us feedback.
I think we're all on Twitter.
If we're not, we should be.
And tag us and let
us know what you
like and don't like about this.
LOGAN KILPATRICK: Don't tag me.
Tag them.
DUMITRU ERHAN: I don't know.
Yeah.
Maybe one limitation that
I have personally observed
is that sometimes editing will
edit more than you asked for.
I think it's almost the opposite
of what you're asking about.
It'll be like-- and that's--
I don't know.
We need to dig deeper into how
and which way is the problem.

under specify what your edit is,
the model will do more than
you thought should be do--
should be done, right?
You may be technically correct.
It did what you did, but
it also did some more.
SHLOMI FRUCHTER: When
it comes to videos,
there's so much happening.
Ten-second video, actually
a lot is happening.
And to be able to edit it
accurately, even explain
what you want, with language
is not always very easy.
So sometimes you might ask
for something to change,
but again, it is
kind of ill-defined.
What's the right thing to do?
Editing is not always clear.
OK, I want to change this
text to something else.
That's one thing.
But if I want to change the--
make it invisible,
there are many ways,
for example, like we've
seen in this violin,
to make it maybe invisible or
change the camera position.
There are multiple ways.
So the more you're
specifying what you want,
I think the better the
model can understand
and try to implement the edit.
But still, of course, it
doesn't always get it right,
and we're still
working on getting it
to be more and more accurate.
LOGAN KILPATRICK: How much
reasoning is actually happening?
Is that part of that 90 seconds,
is the model actually doing
or 60 seconds the
model is actually
doing a bunch of
reasoning similar
to the latter Nano
Banana models, where
that's a core part of how we're
getting model performance out
of it?
GABE BARTH-MARON: Yeah, there
is quite a bit of reasoning
that goes on behind the scenes.
I mean, if you think about when
you're doing text to video,
and you give it a simple
prompt, as you said,
there's a lot more going on in
the video than just like a dog
on a skateboard or
something like that.
Well, where's the dog?
What time of the day
is it, et cetera?
And so the model really needs
to create a lot of detail.
And so it needs to
reason about it,
just like a person creating a
film would reason about, well,
what's the story?
What's going on?
LOGAN KILPATRICK:
And that's actually
what's happening, is it's
reasoning through scene by scene
or something like that?
Or I don't know how much
of this is the secret sauce
or how much is actually even
visible to users at all,
but what happens
as it is thinking
through what the next 8
or 9 seconds of the video
should look like?
SHLOMI FRUCHTER: If you
provide a very short prompt,
then there is so much to create
to just give you a 10-second
video.
So a lot of this information is
coming from the model thinking
through how it should be, maybe
split the 10 seconds or longer
to connect shorter
kind of clips.
What should happen
in each one, how
they should be consistent
with each other--
so there is lots of
planning around that.
And then eventually,
the video that you get
tries to combine all of
this information that
are in this planning
into a coherent video.
So if you provide more
information, for example,
and one thing that I like
is that you can actually
say I want in specific time,
specific seconds for something
to happen, then you constrain
much more the video.
So if you provide
more information,
the model will try and adhere
to what the user wants.
And then, if you
provide less, then it
has to go and be more of
a director on your behalf.
LOGAN KILPATRICK: Nice.
I'm curious why 10 seconds.
Is it just the model has
gotten better and more coherent
or architecturally it's
set up to do 10 seconds?
Or why 10 seconds?
Why not-- I know 30 seconds
would take a long time
to generate.
SHLOMI FRUCHTER: With Omni, you
can create 10-second videos.
That's true.
But because of the consistency,
that using references,
you can easily have the
same basically character
or characters in
a 10 second video.
So you can easily create
a much longer film.
That being said,
we are definitely
planning to extend that
in the near future.
NICOLE BRICHTOVA:
We really tried
to focus on making this
accessible to consumers
with this release.
I think that's quite new,
because with Veo, we really
focused on professional
creators and filmmakers.
And we're still working
with those, obviously,
because everything
that we've shown
you is useful if you're
creating content professionally.
But we really wanted to make
this accessible to consumers.
So the fact that can
create your avatar,
and then you can put
yourself in videos
and it looks like you, that's
kind of that Nano Banana
moment for video.
Shorter videos we also think are
more conducive to the consumer
use cases, but we are planning
on enabling longer videos.
And one interesting
thing is when
we talk to folks who are
creating films professionally,
they actually prefer to have
shorter scenes, because you
create a scene, and then
you stack those scenes.
So the workflow that
Shlomi described
is actually quite
common in the industry.
But you're right.
We do want to make
longer videos,
and that's definitely
on the roadmap.
DUMITRU ERHAN: There's
also a user experience.
Imagine doing a multi-turn
edit of a 90-second video.
Most users will just not
find this very pleasant,
but we could do it as a flag
planting thing if you want.
GABE BARTH-MARON:
We'll get there.
DUMITRU ERHAN: Yeah,
we'll get there.
GABE BARTH-MARON:
We'll get there.

of the things, actually,
that we haven't talked about,
and this is related to use cases
and the different audiences
and everything they're looking
for, maybe we can actually
just talk about availability

people trying to do the Nano
Banana or Veo moment,
where should they be going
for the more professional user
who wants to do the 10-second
multi, many, many iterations,
put together something
professional, where
should they be going--
availability?
NICOLE BRICHTOVA: For
easy consumer use cases,
go to the Gemini app.

and Pro and Plus users.
LOGAN KILPATRICK: Really?
Nice.
NICOLE BRICHTOVA: Yes.
LOGAN KILPATRICK: And that's

NICOLE BRICHTOVA:

this is related, right?

video generations,
then we can serve

a trade-off

more intensive workflows

Flow now has some

LOGAN KILPATRICK:
